name: Communism of property and of the family
plain_explanation: Guardians are to own no private property beyond bare necessities, and are to have no private families: spouses and children are shared in common, with marriages secretly arranged by lottery-manipulating rulers for eugenic purposes, and children raised without knowing their biological parents.
precise_definition: Plato's proposal that the guardian (and possibly soldier) class hold all property in common, live communally like a military camp, and abolish private marriage and parenthood: 'breeding' festivals are rigged by the rulers under cover of a lottery to concentrate reproduction among the 'best' individuals, all children are removed at birth and raised collectively, and kinship terms (father, mother, brother, sister) are extended loosely by age-cohort to preserve social taboos without genetic tracking.
why_it_mattered: Russell treats this as Plato's attempt to eliminate private, possessive emotions that could compete with loyalty to the state, at the acknowledged cost of near-total state control over reproduction and family life.
historical_origin: An extension of the Spartan common-mess and shared-upbringing model, and Russell notes a parallel motive to that behind clerical celibacy.
examples: 'These women shall be, without exception, the common wives of these men, and no one shall have a wife of his own.'
Deformed children and children of inferior parents are to be 'put away in some mysterious unknown place.'
Mothers between twenty and forty, fathers between twenty-five and fifty-five, are the sanctioned reproductive ages; abortion or infanticide is compulsory outside them.
objections: Russell notes that if Plato's own kinship-avoidance rules (no father-daughter or mother-son unions, and generally no brother-sister unions) were followed strictly, they would in fact prohibit virtually all marriages, since almost anyone could plausibly be a 'sibling' under the loose age-based kinship system.
influence_on_later_thinkers: Echoed, per Russell, in the historical practice of clerical celibacy, which sought a similar reduction of private possessive attachment.
